title: What is one factory instance, physically?
body: A factory needs a home for its durable state and the role leaders' terminals. Options: (A) one factory per OS user per host. Leaders and workers all run on that host, and a remote host is a separate factory you run there. (B) One factory per user, with workers spread across several hosts. (C) Several factories per user on one host, such as one per project.
rec: A. One factory per OS user per execution host, installed without root. Local and remote are the same thing with a different host. You can run one locally and one remotely, but they are independent factories that share no state. B needs cross-host leadership and transport, and nothing has qualified that yet.
options: A: one factory per user per host
C: several factories per user per host

title: Which host operating systems does v1 support?
body: The adapter evidence is Linux-only. Each additional OS adds supervisor integration (systemd vs launchd), PTY/terminal-protocol differences, and its own qualification runs.
rec: Linux only for v1 certification, on both local and remote hosts. macOS is out of v1 until it is separately qualified. Windows is out unless running under WSL as Linux.

title: What keeps the agent terminals alive and owns their input?
body: Agents must outlive your terminal and SSH session. Options: (A) an AsmAI daemon owns every provider PTY through the relay contract you already validated. You attach with `asmai attach <agent>`, and the daemon enforces one input owner. (B) tmux hosts the PTYs and AsmAI drives them with send-keys/capture. (C) There is no background process, so agents live only while your `asmai` foreground session runs.
rec: A. A per-user AsmAI daemon owns the PTYs, input fencing, and hook intake. tmux is not required, because send-keys cannot fence human input or confirm submission. Optionally, a user-level systemd unit restarts the daemon. tmux remains something you can run your attach client inside.
options: A: AsmAI daemon owns PTYs (systemd user unit optional)
B: tmux hosts PTYs, AsmAI drives them
C: foreground only, no background process

title: How do you reach a factory on a remote host?
body: This covers the Coordination conversation, attaching to any agent, and Lavish reviews on a remote host. Options: (A) SSH in and run `asmai attach` there. Lavish is reached through SSH port forwarding, and the factory opens no network listener. (B) The factory exposes an authenticated network endpoint (TLS) so a local `asmai` client attaches remotely. (C) Both.
rec: A. SSH only, with no network listener in v1. This avoids AsmAI owning authentication and TLS, and it matches the finding that the same-user relay is not a security boundary. Lavish URLs are printed with the forwarding command you need.
options: A: SSH + local-on-host attach, port-forward Lavish

title: What exactly does 'one leader per role' promise during failures?
body: Research: continuous exactly-one availability can't be promised through crashes. Options: (A) Safety first. At most one process may act as a role's leader at any instant, enforced by fencing so a stale or resumed process is rejected. After a failure the factory restores one leader, with a gap during which the role is leaderless and its work waits. (B) Availability first. Run a standby leader that takes over quickly, which risks overlap without strong fencing.
rec: A. At most one leader per role at any instant. A leaderless gap is acceptable: requests queue durably and nothing that role authorizes proceeds until the leader is restored. There are no standby leaders in v1.
options: A: at most one, with fencing; gap tolerated
B: standby leaders for fast takeover

title: Which failures must v1 recover from?
body: Each tier needs its own acceptance test. Pick the highest tier v1 must survive with work intact, meaning after reconciliation and with no lost assignments or decisions: (1) your terminal or SSH disconnects; (2) one agent process crashes; (3) the daemon crashes; (4) the host reboots; (5) the host is lost and the factory moves to another host.
rec: Through tier 4 (host reboot), using durable on-disk state and reconciliation. Anything uncertain becomes 'needs reconciliation', not a blind retry. Tier 5 (host loss or migration) is out of v1, so back up the state directory yourself.

title: What happens when an agent's input state is unknown (native modal, unexpected prompt)?
body: The Codex rate-limit modal swallowed automated input during the prototype. Options: (A) Never answer unknown modals automatically. The agent pauses with 'input state unknown' and Coordination asks you to intervene, while other work continues. (B) Keep an allow-list of known, qualified modals with a safe default answer, such as dismissing a nudge while keeping the current model, and pause on everything else. (C) Always send Escape or a cancel and retry.
rec: B, but start with an empty allow-list. A modal is added only after it is qualified for that exact runtime version and the answer cannot change provider, model, authentication, or permissions. Everything else pauses and escalates, as in A. C is rejected because it can cancel real work or answer a permission prompt.
options: B: qualified allow-list, else pause (starts empty)
